title: The Guru is the Granth
hookLine: after the Ardas many recite the couplet: by the Timeless One's command the panth was founded, and all Sikhs are to accept the Granth as Guru

lines: A FEW MORE LINES RING OUT.
cards: The Ardas is over. Everyone has bowed. In many gurdwaras, before anyone sits, a few more lines ring out, sung or chanted, often by the whole hall at once.

They aren't a prayer, exactly. They're closer to a reminder, said aloud, of who is in charge here. And who is in charge is right there at the front of the room, under a canopy, wrapped in cloth: a book.

teach.b: The couplet goes, in its best-known form: aagiaa bhai akaal ki, tabhi chalaayo panth. By the command of the Timeless One, the panth, the Sikh community, was set on its way. Sabh sikhan ko hukam hai, guru maaniyo granth.
All Sikhs are commanded: accept the Granth as Guru. It often continues: accept the Guru Granth as the visible body of the Gurus, and whoever wishes to meet the Lord, seek in the Shabad, the Word.
In 1708, at Nanded in the Deccan, Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, was near death.

teach.h: THE LINE OF GURUS PASSES TO THE WORD.
teach.b: Sikh tradition says that instead of naming an eleventh human Guru, he placed the line of Gurus in the scripture, the Adi Granth, from then on called Guru Granth Sahib.
Spiritual authority went to the Word; the Khalsa panth would carry it in the world. The couplet itself isn't from the Guru Granth Sahib.

teach.h: SEEK THE LORD IN THE SHABAD.
teach.b: It's a later verse of the Sikh tradition, and historians discuss exactly when it took this form. But the idea it states is the center of Sikh practice.
That's why, in a gurdwara, the Granth sits higher than anyone, why people bow before it, why it's put to rest at night and opened again at dawn. The respect isn't for paper and ink.
It's for the voice of the Gurus that Sikhs hear in those pages.
So guru maaniyo granth isn't a slogan. It says where to look: for Sikhs, to seek the Guru is to open the Word.

how: After the Ardas, many congregations recite the dohra aagiaa bhai akaal ki… guru maaniyo granth, then bow before the Guru Granth Sahib and raise the jaikara.

o: where the tenth Guru passed Guruship to the Granth
the city where Guru Nanak was born and grew up
the town where the Khalsa was first founded

games.q: the Granth is Guru — tap the pairs.

s: the couplet is a verse from the Guru Granth Sahib
it's a later verse of the tradition; the idea it states is central.
Guru Gobind Singh named an eleventh human Guru
tradition says he placed the Guru's authority in the scripture instead.
the Granth is put to rest at night and opened at dawn
a sign that Sikhs treat it as the living Guru.

games.q: you're Guru Gobind Singh in 1708, near the end. who comes after you?
o: the scripture: the Granth is Guru.
games.why: tradition says he passed the Guruship to the Granth, with the Khalsa panth to carry it in the world.

practice: If you're in a gurdwara, you can bow before the Guru Granth Sahib the way the congregation does; if not, sit quietly and let your head lower a little, slowly, the way you'd nod to a teacher you respect.
Notice what it feels like to bow to wisdom rather than to someone's power, and rest there, breathing, as if waiting for a teacher to speak. If you pray, say Waheguru once as your head comes up.

wordCard.voice: Nanded, where in 1708 Guru Gobind Singh placed the Guru's authority in the scripture: Sikhs call it Guru Granth Sahib, and seek the Guru in its Word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: accept the Granth as the Guru; the line many recite after the Ardas.

carryVoice: Your line: guru maneyo granth. Ten Gurus, and then the Word, from Nanded on. That's day six hundred thirty-six.
